paper_title: Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autonomous agents can increasingly propose ideas, modify code, and run experiments, creating an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery using teams of collaborative AI researchers. To escape local minima in the discovery, we propose to encourage orthogonal exploration by constructing the team using agents with varying expertise. However, realizing this design requires more than diverse backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team can test only a limited number of ideas, thereby creating the need to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting a subset of researchers to propose and execute new experiments. Furthermore, each result should shape what the team tries next. We therefore ask how AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds can build on one another's findings and sustain progress under a limited experimental budget. To address these challenges, we build a team of persistent AI researchers, each grounded in a different discipline, who keep private research histories, share experimental evidence, and receive research opportunities through adaptive allocation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design by deploying the team to search for linear attention architectures, where it outperforms GDN2 at 1.3B scale on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks. In controlled comparisons, removing any single organizational component from our design yields markedly weaker discoveries: without disciplinary backgrounds, the search plateaus early; without private histories, researchers make less progress despite identical shared evidence; and uniform selection falls short of adaptive allocation within the same budget. These results suggest that sustained autonomous discovery depends not only on stronger agents, but also on who explores, what they remember, and how research effort is allocated.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Autonomous agents can increasingly propose ideas, modify code, and run experiments, creating an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery using teams of collaborative AI researchers. To escape local minima in the design space induced by common reasoning patterns, we propose to encourage orthogonal exploration by constructing the team using agents with varying expertise. However, realizing this design requires more than diverse backgrounds. When experiments are costly, team can test only limited number of ideas, thereby creating the need to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting subset of researchers to propose and execute new experiments. Furthermore, each result should shape what the team tries next. The team must decide where to deepen an investigation, when to explore alternatives, and how to carry lessons across researchers. We therefore ask how AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds can build on one anothers findings and sustain progress under limited experimental budget. To address these challenges, we build team of persistent AI researchers, each grounded in different discipline, who keep private research histories, share experimental evidence, and receive research opportunities through adaptive allocation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design by deploying the team to search for linear attention architectures at 150M parameters. We then scale the teams strongest discovery to 1.3B parameters, where it outperforms GDN2 on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks. In controlled comparisons, removing any single organizational component from our design yields markedly weaker discoveries: without disciplinary backgrounds, the search plateaus early; without private histories, researchers make less progress despite identical shared evidence; and uniform selection falls short of adaptive allocation within the same budget. Tracing the discovery shows researchers applying principles from their own fields to refine one anothers ideas. These results suggest that sustained autonomous discovery depends not only on stronger agents, but also on who explores, what they remember, and how research effort is allocated.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Autonomous research agents increasingly connect hypothesis generation, implementation, and experimental evaluation into iterative discovery processes (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025; Schmidgall et al., 2025; Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025; Karpathy, 2026). However, in well-developed fields, progress can enter local minimum when the explored region of the design space is confined. Related efforts investigate how persistent experience and collaboration can support scientific work across multiple agents and repeated investigations (Qu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025a; Swanson et al., 2024). These capabilities create compelling opportunity to encourage diverse exploration by assembling team of AI researchers grounded in different scientific fields, with distinct prior knowledge, conceptual frameworks, and ways of reasoning, and having them work together to push the state-of-the-art on the same open-ended problem. This allows the researchers to leverage mechanism suggested by one field to address limitation recognized in another. For example, advances in linear attention have gained insights from fast-weight learning to build memories that can correct 1 Preprint under review Figure 1: Illustration of collaborative autoresearch. Sixteen research agents with diverse scientific backgrounds collaborate on linear attention architecture search. Starting from Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN2), the team discovers Context-First DeltaNet (CFDN), which improves performance across language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks. stored associations (Schlag et al., 2021). The potential value of such team therefore lies not only in generating more proposals, but in developing ideas through complementary investigations. Realizing this potential, however, requires more than assigning researchers different backgrounds. When experiments are costly, team can test only limited number of ideas and cannot pursue every direction equally deeply. Which directions will prove productive is uncertain, and due to the high cost of conducting an experiment, exploration and exploitation must be balanced when selecting which of the diverse hypotheses proposed by the team to test. Furthermore, an early result may reveal limitation that further work can address. Each experiment therefore does more than test proposal: it produces evidence that can change what its author or another researcher tries next. The team must use that evidence to decide where to deepen an investigation and when to explore alternatives, while carrying useful lessons across researchers and experiments. Existing demonstrations of collaboration and search have not yet established what disciplinary backgrounds and researchers own accumulated experience add to shared evidence, or how research opportunities should be distributed across such team. With these challenges in mind, we therefore ask: how can team of AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds build on one anothers findings and sustain progress on open-ended research problems under limited experimental budget? To address these challenges, we propose an autoresearch pipeline that brings together team of persistent AI researchers, each initialized with different disciplinary profile containing domain knowledge, mathematical tools, scientific insights, and ways to approach research problems. The team conducts an iterative search in which each iteration follows one proposal through independent review and, if approved, implementation and evaluation, ending with its author reflecting on the outcome. To make this process cumulative, researchers retain private histories of their investigations while sharing proposals, outcomes, and lessons with the team. This allows individual researchers to develop line of inquiry over time, while others can revisit its assumptions, extend its mechanisms, or combine its findings with those from another direction. As these lines of inquiry develop, an adaptive scheduler balances further investment in researchers with strong empirical contributions against opportunities for those whose potential is less explored. To ground this team in problem that draws on different scientific perspectives, we choose linear attention architecture discovery. Its central modeling challenge is to retain and use sequence information through fixed-size recurrent state while maintaining model quality and efficient computation (Katharopoulos et al., 2020). Recent advances have explored connections between state-space models and attention, delta-rule updates, channel-wise forgetting, and separately controlled erasing and writing (Dao & Gu, 2024; Yang et al., 2025b;a; Team et al., 2025; Hatamizadeh et al., 2026). These developments illustrate how different perspectives can inform choices about what to remember, how to revise stored information, and how to retrieve it efficiently. Determining which of these choices improve model performance requires implementing and training candidate architectures. The cost of these experiments, in turn, limits how many directions the team can pursue and how deeply it can investigate each one. Building on prior demonstrations that agents can propose, implement, and 2 Preprint under review evaluate architectures (Liu et al., 2025b; Pepe et al., 2026), we therefore use this setting to study how our heterogeneous team organization supports discovery under limited experimental budget. We evaluate this organization at 150M model scale, using Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN2) as the baseline. Proposed candidates receive matched training budgets and are evaluated on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and retrieval tasks. Our strongest discovery, Context-First DeltaNet (CFDN), adds recurrent vector to GDN2s matrix memory, combining query-independent contribution from the vector with query-dependent read from the matrix. We then scale it to 1.3B parameters, where it improves performance in every evaluation category over GDN2. To understand which organizational choices contribute to these discoveries, we conduct controlled ablations on expert-background conditioning, private longitudinal memory, adaptive researcher selection, and evaluator design. Results show that providing disciplinary profiles broadens the mechanisms explored and leads to better architectures than those discovered without these profiles. Private histories support more effective refinement of earlier ideas beyond what is achieved with shared evidence alone. Adaptive selection finds higher-scoring architectures than uniform selection within the same number of research iterations. Optimizing solely for language modeling, however, steers search toward improvements that transfer less consistently across evaluations. We complement these comparisons by tracing how ideas develop across researchers. Figure 1 provides an overview of the trajectories, which reveal connections between researchers scientific backgrounds and the hypotheses they pursue, as well as how they adopt and revise each others ideas using shared experimental evidence. To summarize, our contributions are threefold: We build framework for organizing autonomous research teams under limited compute, combining diverse scientific backgrounds, persistent memory, shared evidence, and adaptive allocation. We discover improved linear attention architectures under matched training compute at 150M scale and evaluate the strongest at 1.3B scale. We link organizational choices to discovery outcomes through controlled comparisons and trajectory analysis, providing guidance for designing autonomous research teams.

sections.title: 2 METHODOLOGY
sections.content: We organize autonomous discovery as collaboration among researchers who bring different scientific perspectives to shared problem, encouraging orthogonal exploration of the design space. The team develops through experience, makes each researchers findings useful to others, and decides where to invest further effort. Figure 2 gives an overview of our design. We first describe the researchers and their individual and shared knowledge, then the iterative process through which they develop and test ideas, where costly experiments create need to balance exploration and exploitation. Finally, we define the experimental feedback that guides our search for linear attention architectures. 2.1 SCIENTIFIC PERSPECTIVES AND ACCUMULATED KNOWLEDGE In many well-researched areas, substantial progress is hindered by the tendency of researchers to explore confined regions of an otherwise broad space of potential designs, creating local minimum. We therefore propose to assemble our AI research team with different disciplinary backgrounds to bring complementary concepts, assumptions, and diagnostic tools to its investigation. Each researcher is an instance of the same language model, with the same tools and common description of the problem, baseline, and experimental constraints. Grounding researchers in scientific backgrounds. Each researcher receives disciplinary profile that develops three kinds of guidance: Prior knowledge and mathematical tools: central objects, equations, assumptions, and representative literature that provide concrete mechanisms to reason with. Scientific insights: when those mechanisms are useful, where familiar intuitions fail, and which apparently similar problems require different explanations. Research habits: ways to decompose an unfamiliar problem, quantities to inspect, and counterexamples that could challenge hypothesis. 3 Preprint under review Figure 2: Organization of the autonomous research team. (a) Sixteen researchers have distinct scientific backgrounds and persistent individual histories. Adaptive selection balances measured contributions with opportunities for less-tested researchers. (b) selected researcher develops one proposal through review and, if approved, implementation and experimentation, then reflects on its outcome. (c) Proposals, outcomes, and their relationships form shared body of knowledge through which researchers build on one anothers work. Circled numbers identify the four organizational factors studied in our comparisons. For example, the Bayesian-filtering profile explains how prediction errors should be interpreted relative to uncertainty and how to distinguish isolated outliers from persistent changes. dynamicalsystems profile emphasizes how repeated transitions preserve or amplify perturbations. streamingalgorithms profile asks which queries bounded summary must support. These perspectives suggest different approaches to the same problem. Appendix C.1 lists the full roster and example profiles. Preserving individual experience. profile is starting point for reasoning. Researchers may still develop their perspectives and insights about how their area of expertise relates to the research problem. To achieve that, each agent retains its session history and private research notes across investigations, preserving hypotheses, the reasoning behind earlier decisions, and reflections on their outcomes. In addition to persisting these derived insights, this continuity allows researcher to revisit an unresolved question or revise an assumption. Making findings useful to others. Private experience alone would leave useful insights confined to their authors. All researchers therefore have access to shared record of proposals, reviews, experimental results, and conclusions. It exposes both what was tried and why, allowing researchers to extend mechanism proposed by others, reconsider an assumption, or combine findings from different investigations. Accumulated findings are synthesized every 10 iterations into shared lessons and unresolved questions. Individual histories and shared knowledge thus support two forms of continuity: developing ones own reasoning and building on discoveries made elsewhere in the team. 2.2 AN ITERATIVE PROCESS FOR DEVELOPING AND TESTING IDEAS With the initialized researchers, the team proposes and evaluates new ideas to approach the problem in an iterative process. Each iteration contains the following steps that turn existing knowledge into new investigation and return its findings to the team. Step 1: Select researcher. Although we would ideally allow all researchers to propose and test diverse ideas in each iteration, this is not tractable in most real-world research settings due to high experimental costs. Therefore, in each iteration, we must first select one researcher from the team to propose new idea. With limited experimental opportunities, repeatedly choosing recent winners can overlook researchers whose ideas have not been sufficiently tested. We therefore use discounted upper confidence bound (UCB) selection (Garivier & Moulines, 2011) to balance exploration and 4 Preprint under review exploitation. Each completed iteration earns nonnegative reward rj for improving on the teams best model known when that iteration began. Section 2.3 defines this reward in detail. The mean reward ri(t) favors researchers with stronger historical contributions, and the second term preserves opportunities for less-tested researchers, with being hyperparameter controlling the strength of exploration. Intuitively, the discount factor γ assigns more weight to recent contributions, thus giving researchers who perform well recently more continuity in developing along their promising directions. Step 2: Propose hypothesis. Selection determines who investigates next, but the researcher decides which scientific direction to pursue. The selected researcher examines its own history and shared experimental results to identify limitation worth investigating. It may develop new mechanism or revise an earlier proposal, including one from another researcher. The proposal states what should change, why that change should help, and which experimental outcome would challenge the hypothesis. For our linear attention architecture discovery, it specifies the mathematical operations and their parameterization, together with parallelizable formulation suitable for training. Step 3: Review the proposal. Before committing training compute, two independent reviewers assess whether the proposed experiment is sound and informative. technical reviewer checks the mathematics and computational feasibility. If these checks pass, second reviewer assesses novelty and research value in light of prior work and the teams findings. rejection leads directly to reflection (Step 6); otherwise, the reviews identify any issues to resolve before testing the proposal. Step 4: Refine the proposal. For proposal that passes review, the author revises its mathematical design in response to the critiques. The author is responsible for resolving the reviewers critiques and providing detailed specification for implementation. If the critiques cannot be addressed without replacing the central mechanism, the author withdraws the proposal and proceeds to reflection. Step 5: Implement, train, and evaluate. separate implementation agent translates the final specification into code and checks that it realizes the intended computation. The implementation must pass integration and speed checks before training. Specifically, we require the implemented models per-step training time to be less than 1.2 times the baseline GDN2 time to prevent architectures that degrade efficiency. Repairable failures are returned to the implementer with diagnostics. Finally, validated candidates are trained from scratch under matched training compute, using the same training data, and evaluated with three metrics defined in Section 2.3. Step 6: Reflect and share. The proposing researcher revisits its original hypothesis in light of the outcome, including rejection or failure. Reviews, implementation, and experimental records are provided to help it distinguish evidence about the mechanism from problems in realizing or testing it. The researcher records what the outcome supports, what remains unresolved, and what it suggests investigating next. It updates its private notes for future reference and shares generalizable lessons with other researchers. Completing this reflection ends the iteration and updates the observations used for researcher selection in future iterations. 2.3 EVALUATING ARCHITECTURES AND REWARDING RESEARCH PROGRESS The evaluation metrics shape both the hypotheses researchers pursue and the reward used by the selection rule. For linear attention discovery, we seek improvements in general model capabilities that span different tasks and scenarios. We therefore evaluate three complementary aspects to measure progress on model quality (details in Appendix B). ❶ Language modeling measures next-token prediction with negative log-likelihood L; lower is better. ❷ Common-sense reasoning measures downstream task performance with mean accuracy Q; higher is better. ❸ Retrieval tests whether information remains accessible from context, using an exact-continuation proxy on the synthetic needle-in-a-haystack tasks; higher is better. sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Our experiments answer three questions: can the team discover useful architectures; which organizational choices help in the limited-iteration setting; and how do different researchers contribute to successful discovery? We first describe the experiment settings, then evaluate the discovered architecture, compare research organizations, and trace the development of the found architecture. 3.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETTING Research team. We use 16 researchers and budget of 80 research iterations. All agent roles use GPT-6 Astra with high reasoning effort through the Codex harness. We allow maximum of 8 researchers working in parallel, while forcing their proposal stage to be sequential to prevent repetition in proposed ideas. In the first 16 iterations, all researchers are invoked exactly once, and further researcher selection is based on the UCB rule. Model backbones and search space. We search at approximately 150M non-embedding parameters, and we scale the discovered best candidate to 1.3B parameters. We use GDN2 (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) as the baseline. Candidates can change the recurrent mixers memory representation, update rule, readout, and parameterization, while retaining the common depth, residual width, and feedforward network. We also compare with Gated DeltaNet (GDN) (Yang et al., 2025a) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) (Team et al., 2025) using the same surrounding architecture. Appendix gives the dimensions and parameter-count convention at both scales. Training data and budget. All models are trained from scratch on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024). For all models, we adjust their training tokens to match the total FLOPs of training GDN: at 150M scale, we train GDN for 15B tokens; at 1.3B scale, we train GDN for 100B tokens. More expensive architectures therefore receive fewer training tokens. Following Hatamizadeh et al. (2026), all models use the same optimizer hyperparameters and global batch size (details in Appendix A). Final evaluation and search feedback. We evaluate models on language modeling (LM), commonsense reasoning (CSR), synthetic needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH), and, for 1.3B models, in-context real-world retrieval (RWR) tasks. For LM, we report perplexity on WikiText (Wiki.) (Merity et al., 2016) and LAMBADA (LMB.) (Paperno et al., 2016). For CSR, we report the mean accuracy over eight datasets (Bisk et al., 2019; Zellers et al., 2019; Sakaguchi et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2018; Mihaylov et al., 2018; Sap et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019). For NIAH, we use four synthetic tasks (S-NIAH-1, 2, 3 and MK-NIAH) from RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024). For in-context real-world retrieval, we report mean accuracy over six datasets (Arora et al., 2025; Rajpurkar et al., 2018; Joshi et al., 2017; Kwiatkowski et al., 2019; Dua et al., 2019). During search, we use reduced suite to provide feedback: LM loss on the same two datasets, subset of 256 examples from each CSR dataset, and 64 examples per NIAH task at each of 1K, 2K, and 4K context. We do not evaluate RWR during search. The NIAH evaluation uses teacher-forced continuation proxy instead of answer generation. sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Autonomous research agents. growing line of work automates the iterative research process from hypothesis to experiment, through fixed pipelines from idea generation to written paper (Lu et al., 2024; Schmidgall et al., 2025), agentic tree search (Yamada et al., 2025), or evolutionary search with the language model as the mutation operator (Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025). In these works, single agent or fixed pipeline proposes every candidate. Other work organizes team of researchers around shared scientific problem. These teams differ in how they are composed, what each member retains and what the team shares, and how research opportunities are distributed. VirSci, ASCollab, and ScienceClaw (Su et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026) give agents distinct backgrounds, personas, or scientific profiles. CORAL (Qu et al., 2026), ASCollab, and ScienceClaw keep long-running agents with their own histories and shared record, whereas AgentRxiv (Schmidgall & Moor, 2025) starts fresh laboratory instance per project that reads shared archive of earlier papers. However, none compares teams with and without different backgrounds on the outcomes of implementing, training, and evaluating what they propose, or tests whether private memory adds anything once findings are shared. Adaptive allocation itself is not new, but no existing work both gives researchers different backgrounds and allocates opportunities among them adaptively. The Virtual Lab (Swanson et al., 2024) decides which specialist takes an agenda item, ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2025) decides which language model performs the next mutation, SwarmResearch (Virk et al., 2026) decides which branch of the search to extend, and Economy of Minds (Qi et al., 2026) decides which agent acts next in task. Each of them chooses an operator or candidate to advance. In our setting, the decision is which researcher proposes and tests the next idea, and because each researcher brings its own background and record of what it has tried and learned, that choice determines what evidence the team will have next. No prior team of researchers with different backgrounds makes this decision adaptively. Autonomous research has also been applied to architecture design. NADER (Yang et al., 2024b) coordinates fixed-role agents that propose changes to tree of prior modifications. AIRA-Compose and AIRA-Design (Pepe et al., 2026) pool designs from independent search agents, and ASI-Arch (Liu et al., 2025b) runs researcher, engineer, and analyst pipeline over linear attention architectures and reports that discoveries grow with compute. These systems use fixed-role workflows or independent agent searches; we instead fix the experimental budget and vary the organization, comparing who proposes, what they retain and share, who receives the next opportunity, and what counts as progress. Linear attention. Linear attention replaces the key-value cache of softmax attention with fixed-size recurrent state (Katharopoulos et al., 2020), and subsequent designs mainly differ in what the state remembers, how stored information is revised, and how it is retrieved. On what to remember, most designs keep matrix of keyvalue associations, while Titans (Behrouz et al., 2024) replaces it with network learned at inference. On how to revise, RetNet (Sun et al., 2023) decays the state at fixed rate, GLA and Mamba-2 (Yang et al., 2024a; Dao & Gu, 2024) make the decay inputdependent, DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025b) replaces additive writes with delta-rule correction, GDN and KDA (Yang et al., 2025a; Team et al., 2025) combine the delta rule with learned and fine-grained gating, and GDN2 (Hatamizadeh et al., 2026) separates erasing from writing with channel-wise gates. On how to retrieve, MesaNet (von Oswald et al., 2026) solves the regression to optimality at every step, and Parallax (Zuo et al., 2026) restores the intercept of the underlying regression. Each of these works changes one or two choices along these axes, and the space they leave open is large, which makes linear attention architecture discovery natural problem for an autonomous research team.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We study how to organize autonomous researchers for cumulative discovery under limited experimental budgets. Our framework combines diverse scientific backgrounds, persistent memory, shared evidence, and adaptive allocation of research opportunities. Applied to linear attention, the team discovered CFDN, which improves over GDN2 at two scales. Organizational comparisons and research trajectories highlight the importance of heterogeneous agents, adaptive allocation, and shared experimental records. GDN2 uses separate full projections for queries, keys, values, and channel-wise erase and write gates. Query, key, and value projections are followed by causal depthwise convolutions of width four and SiLU; queries and keys are L2-normalized. Decay and output-gate preactivations use two linear maps with bottleneck width 128. The recurrent read is RMS-normalized per head, multiplied by sigmoid output gate, and projected back to the residual stream. Our KDA comparison shares these surrounding components and initialization but uses one scalar erase/write gate per head; GDN additionally uses scalar rather than channel-wise state decay. sections.content: C.1 SCIENTIFIC PROFILES AND RESEARCHER INITIALIZATION The team uses 16 fixed disciplinary profiles. Each is self-contained document of approximately 2,0002,300 words, combining fields mathematical foundations, design judgments, diagnostic practices, and primary references. Table 13 summarizes the different research questions these documents foreground. Appendix C.3 reproduces the complete Bayesian-filtering profile supplied to one researcher. Only the focal linear attention profile is written specifically about the target architecture family. At initialization, each researcher receives one profile, the common problem statement, and access to shared references covering the baseline, prior work, and experimental constraints. Its conversation, private notebook, and earlier proposal dossiers preserve individual experience as the search proceeds. At each new assignment, the researcher additionally receives summary of previous results, ongoing investigations, and consolidated shared lessons, with access to the underlying records. The fixed profile therefore supplies an initial technical perspective, while private and shared evidence can change the researchers subsequent judgments. Table 13: The 16 scientific perspectives. Each row summarizes one profiles organizing question; it is not prescribed candidate mechanism or an exclusive research territory. Scientific perspective Organizing question or distinction Conditional routing and adaptive computation Multiscale and hierarchical recurrence Stable, switched, and non-normal dynamics Multiplicative operators and automata Parallel and I/O-aware recurrent design Streaming sketches and mergeable summaries Cache policies and memory hierarchies Differentiable computers and neural data structures Predictive representations and information bottlenecks Bayesian filtering and regime change Continual memory and consolidation Associative and sparse adaptive memory Vector-symbolic structured memory Tensor, spectral, and low-rank operator memory Online recurrent learning and eligibility traces Linear attention and recurrent matrix memory When should state change, which path should act, and when is further computation worthwhile? How should clocks, temporal boundaries, and communication represent phenomena at different rates? Which distinctions survive input-driven transitions, and when do perturbations amplify? What computations can input-selected operators express through composition? Which algebraic structure permits efficient execution once state traffic and differentiation are counted? Which queries must bounded state support, and how does error compose across updates and merges? What deserves residency, when should it move, and when is stored copy no longer useful? Do learned addressing, allocation, and traversal retain their meaning under repeated operations? Which distinctions in history matter for future predictions, and which can be discarded? How should uncertainty determine correction, and how can an outlier be distinguished from change of regime? How can new information be acquired without overwriting useful prior structure? How do retrieval, residual competition, and allocation interact under finite capacity? Which binding, superposition, and cleanup operations preserve compositional meaning? What state rank preserves distinctions needed by future computations? How can delayed credit be assigned with bounded storage and causal updates? How should fixed-size matrix state read, write, correct, and forget while supporting parallel training? 19 Preprint under review C.2 RESEARCH PROTOCOL AND ANALYSIS DETAILS Proposal and review details. Bayesian Filtering, Innovations, and Regime Change (researcher profile) # Bayesian Filtering, Innovations, and Regime Change Sequential inference is the discipline of maintaining calibrated belief about an evolving latent process. The state of filter is not merely its current best estimate. It is probability distribution--or controlled approximation to one--whose uncertainty determines how new evidence should be interpreted. Consider the state-space model [ x_tsim p(x_tmid x_{t-1}),qquad y_tsim p(y_tmid x_t). ] Bayesian filtering alternates prediction and correction: [ p(x_tmid y_{1:t-1}) =int p(x_tmid x_{t-1})p(x_{t-1}mid y_{1:t-1}),dx_{t-1}, ] [ p(x_tmid y_{1:t}) propto p(y_tmid x_t)p(x_tmid y_{1:t-1}). ] This recursion is exact as an identity. All difficulty lies in representing and updating the posterior. ## Linear-Gaussian filtering and the meaning of innovation For linear dynamics and Gaussian noise, [ x_t=F_tx_{t-1}+w_t,quad w_tsimmathcal N(0,Q_t), ] [ y_t=H_tx_t+v_t,quad v_tsimmathcal N(0,R_t), ] the posterior remains Gaussian. After predicting mean (m_t^-) and covariance (P_t^-), the innovation and its covariance are [ nu_t=y_t-H_tm_t^-,qquad C_t=H_tP_t^-H_t^top+R_t. ] The Kalman gain (K_t=P_t^-H_t^top C_t^{-1}) balances model confidence against measurement confidence, and the corrected mean is (m_t=m_t^-+K_tnu_t). 21 Preprint under review The key quantity is the **normalized innovation**, not the raw residual. residual of magnitude ten is unremarkable if predicted uncertainty is one hundred and alarming if uncertainty is one tenth. Innovation whiteness is also diagnostic: persistent temporal structure in normalized innovations signals misspecified dynamics model, observation model, or noise covariance. Covariance is computational state, not decorative metadata. Discarding it forces fixed response to evidence and prevents principled fusion of measurements with different reliability. Square-root filters propagate factors of (P) for numerical stability. Information-form filters propagate precision (J=P^{-1}) and information vector (h=Jm), making independent measurement contributions additive. Choice of form should follow sparsity and conditioning. Consistency can be tested statistically. Under the assumed model, the normalized innovation squared [ operatorname{NIS}_t=nu_t^top C_t^{-1}nu_t ] has chi-squared reference distribution with dimension equal to the observation dimension. sequence of values that is systematically too large indicates overconfidence or mismatch; values that are systematically too small indicate excessive uncertainty. Temporal dependence must be checked separately with innovation-whiteness tests. Coverage and whiteness reveal failures that root-mean-square error cannot. Even algebraically equivalent covariance updates differ in finite precision. The compact expression (P_t=(I-K_tH_t)P_t^-) can lose symmetry or positive semidefiniteness. The Joseph form, [ P_t=(I-K_tH_t)P_t^-(I-K_tH_t)^top+K_tR_tK_t^top, ] is more robust, and square-root implementations are preferable when conditioning is severe. Numerical representation is part of the inferential method because an invalid covariance implies invalid confidence. ## Beyond single Gaussian Extended Kalman filtering linearizes nonlinear dynamics locally and can become inconsistent when curvature is strong. Sigma-point methods propagate designed set of points through the nonlinear map, improving moment approximation without explicit Jacobians but still reducing the posterior to Gaussian. Particle filters retain weighted samples: [ p(x_tmid y_{1:t})approx sum_{i=1}^{N}w_t^{(i)}delta(x_t-x_t^{(i)}). ] 22 Preprint under review They can represent multimodality and non-Gaussian tails, but importance weights degenerate over time. Resampling removes low-weight particles yet causes impoverishment and destroys ancestry diversity. The importance-sampling distribution is therefore central: sampling only from the transition prior wastes particles when the observation is informative. Differentiable or learned filters do not abolish these issues; they can simply hide miscalibration inside an expressive learned sampler. Rao-Blackwellization is often preferable to brute-force particles. If part of the model is conditionally linear-Gaussian, integrate that part analytically and sample only the discrete or nonlinear component. Expert design exploits conditional structure before increasing particle count. ## Robustness is modeling decision An unexpectedly large innovation admits several explanations: the observation may be corrupted, the latent state may have moved farther than expected, the dynamics may have changed regime, or the posterior may simply have been overconfident. robust filter should not collapse these explanations into one generic downweighting rule. Each implies different posterior and different prediction for the next observation. Heavy-tailed likelihoods, such as Student-(t) observation models, reduce the leverage of isolated outliers. Mixture likelihoods can carry an explicit contamination indicator. Adaptive process noise can accommodate gradual drift, while switching dynamics or run-length uncertainty represent persistent structural change. These mechanisms are not interchangeable. An overly heavy tail can explain away genuine change point forever; inflated process noise can preserve tracking error at the cost of uninformative uncertainty; reset rule can mistake one sensor fault for new regime. distinguish these cases through persistence and cross-channel structure. single-channel spike with immediate recovery supports contamination. Coherent innovations across several measurements support latent motion or model error. sustained change in the distribution of normalized innovations supports regime hypothesis. Posterior predictive checks should reproduce not only marginal residual magnitudes but also their temporal dependence, direction, and coincidence across sensors. Robustness must remain calibrated. method that never issues confident posterior is difficult to falsify but not useful. report coverage conditioned on nominal periods, outliers, and transitions, together with detection delay 23 Preprint under review and false-alarm rate. This makes explicit whether apparent resilience comes from correct hypothesis management or from indiscriminately broad intervals. ## Switching models and hypothesis management Abruptly changing systems require uncertainty over both continuous state and discrete regime. If mode (z_t) follows Markov chain and each mode has its own dynamics, exact filtering yields mixture whose number of components grows exponentially. The interacting multiple-model method controls this explosion by mixing, filtering within each mode, and merging hypotheses at every step. This is an important general lesson: bounded inference requires deliberate **hypothesis management policy**. Pruning, merging, and moment matching are not implementation afterthoughts; they determine which alternative explanations survive. mode with low current probability may need preservation if it predicts high-consequence future or is difficult to recover after deletion. ## Change points as uncertainty over run length Bayesian online change-point detection introduces the run length (r_t), the number of observations since the most recent change. hazard function (H(r)) specifies the prior probability of change after run of length (r). The posterior update combines two possibilities: [ p(r_t=0, y_{1:t}) =sum_{r_{t-1}} p(r_{t-1},y_{1:t-1})H(r_{t-1}) p(y_tmid r_{t-1}), ] and growth transitions (r_t=r_{t-1}+1) weighted by (1-H(r_{t-1})). This is more informative than reset score. It maintains uncertainty over when the current regime began, and each run-length hypothesis carries its own sufficient statistics. The hazard encodes duration assumptions; constant hazard implies geometric regime duration and is often adopted without justification. Exact run-length support grows by one at every observation. bounded implementation must prune, merge, or aggregate old hypotheses, and this approximation determines the longest change history the detector can express. Keeping only the most probable run length turns posterior inference into brittle winner-take-all segmentation. small tail mass spread over many long runs can matter even when no individual run is likely. Outliers and change points are easily confused. robust observation model should explain isolated anomalies without resetting the regime, whereas sustained predictive failure should transfer mass toward short run lengths. Heavy-tailed likelihoods, explicit outlier indicators, and hierarchical hazards help separate these phenomena. ## Event-triggered inference Preprint under review In sensing and networked control, communication or correction can be triggered only when the innovation is informative enough to justify its cost. Crucially, silence can itself be evidence: if sensor transmits only when residual leaves known region, no transmission tells the estimator that the residual remained inside that region. Treating skipped updates as missing at random loses information and biases uncertainty. Event policies should therefore be designed jointly with the estimator. threshold on (nu_t^top C_t^{-1}nu_t) has statistical interpretation, while threshold on raw magnitude does not. Resource-aware filtering asks for an optimal trade between posterior risk, sensing cost, latency, and energy. ## Filtering, smoothing, and decision delay Filtering estimates (x_t) from (y_{1:t}); smoothing permits later observations. Fixed-lag smoothing occupies useful middle ground: it delays commitment by (L) steps and revises recent states using (y_{t+1:t+L}). This is often more valuable than making much larger causal filter, especially near regime boundaries. The correct comparison therefore fixes decision latency. Zero-lag detection, fixed-lag revision, and retrospective segmentation answer different questions. change-point method should also state whether it estimates the first affected sample, the time at which evidence became sufficient, or the time at which an alarm was issued. ## Failure modes - **Overconfidence:** underestimated (Q) or (R) produces brittle gains and poor coverage. - **Model mismatch:** precise posterior under the wrong model is worse than an honest broad posterior. - **Innovation misuse:** large raw residuals are treated as changes without uncertainty normalization. - **Particle collapse:** nominally multimodal filter effectively contains one duplicated hypothesis. - **Premature merging:** distinct modes with similar current means have incompatible futures. - **Hazard misspecification:** expected regime duration silently dictates detection latency. - **Numerical loss of positive definiteness:** naïve covariance updates accumulate roundoff error. - **Retrospective leakage:** smoothing results are reported as if available to an online filter. ## An expert workflow for sequential inference When sequential estimator fails, first decide which problem it is failing to solve. State estimation asks where the process is within trusted model. Robust inference asks whether an observation is an outlier. Model selection asks which dynamics explain the data. Change-point detection asks whether the old regime has ended. These explanations can produce the same large residual, but they imply different updates. My operating sequence is: Preprint under review 1. **Write the belief state.** state which variables are uncertain and which approximation represents their joint posterior: moments, information parameters, particles, regime mixtures, run lengths, or factorization. point estimate is acceptable only when uncertainty cannot affect any subsequent decision. 2. **Predict before observing.** The transition model produces predictive distribution, not just predicted mean. Its spread is the reference against which the next observation becomes ordinary or surprising. 3. **Correct by relative evidence.** inspect likelihood ratios or normalized innovations. Raw residual magnitude has no context. With Gaussian observations, (nu_t^top C_t^{-1}nu_t) is the natural scalar diagnostic; for non-Gaussian models, posterior predictive checks play the same role. 4. **Keep explanations alive when their futures differ.** low-probability regime, run length, or particle family should not be merged merely because its present mean resembles the winner. Pruning is resource decision about tail mass, recoverability, and future consequence. Conditional analytic structure should be Rao-Blackwellized before particles are multiplied. 5. **Interpret persistence.** One unlikely observation may call for heavy-tailed likelihood or outlier indicator. sequence of structured innovations suggests dynamics mismatch or regime change. The hazard model states how readily persistent failure becomes reset; it should never be an invisible constant. 6. **Choose commitment latency.** Filtering, fixed-lag smoothing, and retrospective segmentation permit different evidence. compare methods at equal delay and distinguish the first affected time, the time evidence became sufficient, and the alarm time. 7. **Audit numerical and statistical consistency.** preserve symmetry and positive semidefiniteness with square-root or Joseph-form updates when needed. check posterior coverage, normalized-innovation distributions, innovation whiteness, effective particle diversity, and recovery after mismatch--not point error alone. Missingness and silence require an observation model too. If sensor reports only outside threshold region, no report truncates the residual distribution and is informative. If observations are missing for external reasons, treating the gap as evidence is wrong. Sensing, communication, and inference policies must therefore be specified jointly whenever reporting depends on latent 26 Preprint under review state or innovation. To falsify an estimator, vary noise scale, inject isolated heavy-tailed outliers, switch among regimes with similar current means but different dynamics, alter regime duration, and withhold informative observations. check whether uncertainty broadens before errors grow, whether alternative hypotheses survive long enough to recover, and whether apparent calibration comes from inflating (Q) or (R) to conceal model-form error. Learned dynamics, observation models, and samplers are useful only if their flexibility does not make these checks vacuous; epistemic uncertainty and irreducible observation noise should not be collapsed into one convenient variance. The unresolved resource problem is hypothesis management. Exact belief support usually grows, while hard winner-take-all truncation is brittle. Pruning, merging, moment matching, and learned sampling mechanisms should be judged by which future distinctions they erase and how their lost tail mass is accounted for. The defining principle is that an observation has no fixed importance. Its importance is the likelihood ratio it induces relative to the current predictive belief. ## Selected primary references - Kalman, [A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3662552). - Gordon, Salmond, and Smith, [Novel Approach to Nonlinear/Non-Gaussian Bayesian State Estimation](https://people.bord eaux.inria.fr/pierre.delmoral/gordon-salmond-smith-1993.pdf). - Blom and Bar-Shalom, [The Interacting Multiple Model Algorithm for Systems with Markovian Switching Coefficients](https://doi.org/10.1109/9.1299). - Adams and MacKay, [Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.3742). - Jonschkowski et al., [Differentiable Particle Filters](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11122).
